headline: Stellwagen Edge in 120 feet: cod scattered on gravel, haddock steady on the mud
subhead: Bait-rich water and whale sign are holding bluefin over Tillies Bank while the groundfish bite settles into its early-fall rhythm.
body_markdown:
The gravel edge along Stellwagen Edge, running 105 to 130 feet, is still producing cod, but it's a moving target this week — you find a pod of fish holding on a hard patch, work it for twenty minutes, and then you're picking up the anchor and running again. That's typical for early September. The bait is starting to shift as sand eels thin out and mackerel schools bunch up tighter over the high spots, and the cod are following the food, not sitting still on the same rock pile they held on in August. Haddock have been the more dependable call — they're stacked on the softer mud bottom in that same depth band, 110 to 125 feet, and they're not moving nearly as much. If you want a bend in the rod without burning half a tank running around, mud bottom haddock is the play right now.

We flagged last week that bluefin would stay within reach on the Bank with whale activity marking the bait, and that's exactly how it's played out. Humpbacks and fin whales have been working over mackerel schools on the eastern side of Stellwagen and out toward Tillies Bank, and where the whales are boiling bait to the surface, the tuna aren't far behind. It's not a wide-open bite — this is scattered, opportunistic fish jumping on pushed-up bait, not a stacked pack sitting on a temperature break — but boats running spreads of green machines and small ballyhoo behind the whale activity have been connecting, and the jig-and-pop crews throwing stick baits into visible surface commotion have had shots too. The pattern holds as long as the mackerel stay concentrated, and right now they are.

Water's doing what it does this time of year — cooling from the top down, still comfortable enough to hold bait and fish shallow in the afternoons, but you can feel the season turning underneath it. That thermal squeeze is part of why the whale and tuna activity has been consistent: bait gets pinned against the thermocline and pushed to the surface, and everything with fins shows up to eat. It won't last into October the way it's running now, so this is a window worth using while it's open.

On the groundfish side, the gravel-versus-mud split is the story of the week. Cod on the gravel edges have wanted a diamond jig worked with a short hop-and-drop, or a bait rig with fresh clam threaded on a 6/0 hook, fished right on bottom where the current sweeps the hard patches. Boats jigging have done better than boats just soaking bait when the fish are actively feeding, but when the bite goes quiet, dropping back to fresh clam or herring chunks on a high-low rig has salvaged more than one slow stretch. Haddock on the mud have been eating clam and herring on smaller hooks — a 3/0 to 4/0 on a two-hook bottom rig, 130-pound leader, with just enough weight to hold in the current. These fish aren't picky right now, but they do want the bait fresh, not warmed-over stuff that's been sitting in the cooler since the last trip.

Pollock have been mixed in on both bottom types, mostly as a bycatch on the jig, and a few boats working the edges have picked at hake in the deeper cuts off Stellwagen Basin where the bottom drops into softer structure. Nothing to build a trip around, but worth keeping a rod rigged light if you're anchored up and the cod and haddock go quiet for a stretch.

Tide has been the swing factor for where the bite turns on. The stronger the current sweep across the gravel, the better the cod have fed — dead slack water has been the dead zone, no pun avoided, where boats have had to wait it out or move looking for current still moving somewhere else on the Bank. Plan trips around the building tide rather than the peak of it; the last two hours of a building current into the top of the tide has been the most consistent window boats have reported.

Looking at the next few days, wind is the thing to watch. If it stays manageable out of the west and northwest, boats should keep working both patterns — running the gravel for cod when there's a decent push of current, and sitting on the mud for haddock when it's calmer. The tuna game plan doesn't change: find the whales, find the bait balls pushed to the surface, and work the edges of that activity rather than trying to blind-troll open water. If the wind swings around and builds out of the southeast, that whale and bait activity tends to scatter and push deeper, and the tuna bite gets tougher to find on the surface — worth having trolling gear rigged as a backup if the topwater window closes.

Bottom line for the week ahead: haddock on the mud is the safe, repeatable trip if you want fish in the cooler without a lot of running around. Cod on the gravel is there but requires moving to stay on them. And the bluefin are still catchable if you're willing to run out toward Tillies Bank and work the whale sign — just don't expect it to be a slam dunk every trip. The bait's concentrated enough right now to keep all three patterns alive through the week, but that fall cooldown is coming, and it'll reshuffle things before long.
